title: Computer Security Systems: Defensive Mechanisms and Operational Assurance

stageOutcomes.outcome: Explain trust boundaries, identity, sessions and cryptographic protections in a scoped local service.
stageOutcomes.evidence: An authorized-lab charter, threat model, permission matrix and tested authentication/TLS boundary using synthetic identities.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Explain and verify OS, hardware, network, endpoint and application/database controls.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A least-privilege lab baseline with firewall/IDS observations and positive/negative application tests.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Audit browser/API ownership, cloud policy, secrets, supply-chain provenance and detection coverage.
stageOutcomes.evidence: An ASVS-linked verification matrix, offline IAM cases, secret-rotation drill and labelled detection fixtures.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Operate incident response, tested restoration and risk governance for an evidence-backed security architecture.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A defended local-service capstone, timed recovery drill, risk/exception register and reviewer handover. This is not a certification.

resources.title: OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet
resources.license: Official public guidance; linked rather than redistributed
resources.notes: Use System Modeling, threat identification, mitigations and review to answer what is protected and how. All exercises target only an owned, isolated lab with synthetic data.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4: Authentication and Authenticator Management
resources.license: Official US government publication; link-only here
resources.notes: Current revision 4, final 2025; supersedes the earlier SP 800-63B. Public HTML covers assurance, authenticator requirements, lifecycle and sessions. Use as technical guidance, not a claim of legal compliance or certification.

resources.title: OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet
resources.notes: Authentication and authorization are distinct. Read least privilege, deny by default and permission validation on every request. Test only synthetic users/resources in the local service.

resources.title: OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet
resources.notes: Session identity, lifecycle, cookie attributes, renewal and expiration. Never collect real cookies or credentials for an exercise.

resources.title: OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet
resources.notes: Architecture, data minimization, authenticated encryption and key handling. Use maintained libraries rather than implementing cryptographic primitives. Recheck current algorithm guidance when applying outside the lab.

resources.title: OWASP Transport Layer Security Cheat Sheet
resources.notes: Server configuration, certificates and client authentication. Local test CA trust must remain per-process or inside a disposable lab; never disable certificate verification or change the host's trust store.

resources.title: Linux kernel documentation: Linux Security Module Usage
resources.notes: LSM enforcement hooks, MAC implementations and active-module inspection. Kernel/version details vary. Do not disable controls or alter the host system for these exercises.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn: Secure the Windows boot process
resources.notes: The historical URL covers Windows 10 and Windows 11 mechanisms. Use Secure Boot, Trusted Boot and Measured Boot concepts; it does not endorse running an unsupported OS. No firmware/key changes or paid Windows installation are required.

resources.title: RFC 1034: Domain Names - Concepts and Facilities
resources.license: Official public standards reference; link-only here
resources.notes: Foundational 1987 DNS architecture reference: domain names, name servers, resolvers and caching. Historical examples are not current operational settings. Modern DNSSEC concepts are complemented by RFC 4033; neither requires an account.

resources.title: RFC 4033: DNS Security Introduction and Requirements
resources.license: Official public standards reference; link-only here
resources.notes: Sections 3-4 explain services DNSSEC provides and does not provide. Use the conceptual authenticity/confidentiality distinction, not historical algorithm choices as deployment guidance.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1: Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy
resources.license: Official US government publication; link-only here
resources.notes: September 2009 historical architecture/policy reference, not current product configuration or cipher advice. Open the full publication from its official page on demand. Use current platform documentation for any lab settings.

resources.title: Suricata User Guide: Rules Format
resources.notes: Action, header, protocol/direction and rule options. Use only benign, self-generated lab traffic or synthetic events. No public scanning, attack payload, evasion or third-party packet capture is assigned.

resources.title: OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet
resources.notes: HTTPS, access control, token validation, input/content-type handling and security headers. Use a small owned local API; no external target testing.

resources.title: AWS IAM: Policy evaluation logic
resources.notes: Policy unions/intersections, explicit deny and boundaries. Exercises are offline policy tables, not AWS provisioning. No cloud account, billing change or permission change is needed; simplified exercises are not full AWS authorization emulators.

resources.title: OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
resources.notes: Lifecycle, least privilege, rotation, revocation and audit. Use disposable dummy values only; never inspect, copy or print actual credentials in a learning artifact.

resources.title: SLSA v1.1: Security levels
resources.notes: Pinned v1.1 build-track overview: provenance, hosted-build signing and hardened builds. A learner-generated manifest alone does not establish a SLSA level or certify dependencies.

resources.title: OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet
resources.notes: Event attributes, sensitive-data exclusion, verification and protection of logs. Build original synthetic fixtures rather than collecting real user activity.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
resources.license: Official US government publication; link-only here
resources.notes: Final April 2025, superseding Rev. 2. Read the public overview and linked full publication's CSF 2.0-aligned recommendations. Regulatory reporting obligations remain jurisdiction-specific; no live incident is created.

resources.title: CISA: #StopRansomware Guide
resources.notes: Read prevention and response/recovery checklists, especially offline backups and tested restoration. Labs simulate missing or corrupted copies of synthetic data; never run ransomware, malware or destructive payloads.

resources.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0
resources.notes: Use the CSF 2.0 core, profiles and quick-start material linked from this official hub. Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover are outcomes, not a certification checklist.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture
resources.license: Official US government publication; link-only here
resources.notes: August 2020 architecture reference. Read the linked publication's tenets and logical components; no vendor product, cloud deployment or compliance claim is required.

resources.title: CS50 Cybersecurity: Week 0 - Securing Accounts
resources.license: Official course viewing; recording redistribution not asserted
resources.notes: Verified official week page and topic list. Lecture viewing is free; edX submission/certification is not required. Study defenses only and do not reproduce credential-theft demonstrations.

resources.title: CS50 Cybersecurity: Week 2 - Securing Systems
resources.license: Official course viewing; recording redistribution not asserted
resources.notes: TLS, certificates, VPNs, firewalls and endpoint defenses. External demonstrations are conceptual only; this track does not assign scanning, intrusion or malware execution.

resources.title: CS50 Cybersecurity: Week 3 - Securing Software
resources.license: Official course viewing; recording redistribution not asserted
resources.notes: Use prepared statements, validation, encoding and software-update discussions. No copied attack exercises, real-target probes, exploitation or evasion are assigned.

resources.title: Stanford: Dan Boneh's free online cryptography lectures
resources.license: Official free viewing; no redistribution permission asserted
resources.notes: The official page provides free lectures without Coursera enrollment. Named topics include message integrity, authenticated encryption, key exchange and digital signatures. Historical algorithm examples are not current deployment recommendations.

modules.title: 01. Security objectives and an authorized lab
modules.description: Define what must be protected, from whom, under which explicit authorization and recovery boundary.

lessons.title: Define assets, security goals and safe practice scope
objectives: Distinguish confidentiality, integrity, availability and privacy.
Establish an owned, isolated lab with explicit exclusions and stop conditions.

topics.title: Security goals
details: A control protects a particular property against stated threats.
Protecting confidentiality alone does not ensure correctness or recovery.

topics.title: Authorization
details: Ownership or explicit permission defines the testing boundary.
Synthetic identities and host-only/loopback services prevent contact with real targets.

reading.locator: Overview and System Modeling: answer what is being built and what security properties matter before considering controls.

assignment.title: A defensive lab charter
instructions: Define a fictional notes service containing only generated users and notes, accessible on loopback or an owned host-only VM network.
List assets, permitted actions, excluded networks/data and conditions requiring an immediate stop.
Specify snapshot/backup and teardown steps; no public scans, stolen credentials, malware, evasion or production configuration changes are permitted.
acceptanceCriteria: Every endpoint and dataset is explicitly owned or authorized and isolated.
Confidentiality, integrity and availability each have an observable requirement.
Recovery and cleanup are planned before lab changes.

questions.prompt: Which activity fits this track's scope?
choices: Trying credentials on a public service
Testing synthetic users in your isolated local service
Scanning an employer network without permission
questions.answer: Testing synthetic users in your isolated local service
questions.explanation: Practice requires explicit authorization, isolation and synthetic data. Public accessibility or curiosity is not permission.

questions.prompt: Give an integrity requirement distinct from confidentiality.
questions.answer: For example, only the authorized note owner can change a note and every accepted change is recorded correctly.
questions.explanation: Preventing unauthorized reading and preventing unauthorized or incorrect modification are separate properties.

reviewPrompts: What exact boundary would make you stop the exercise?

lessons.title: Draw data flows and explain trust boundaries
objectives: Identify where inputs, identity and authority cross boundaries.
Link threats to mechanisms, residual risk and verification evidence.

topics.title: System modelling
details: Browsers, services, databases and administrators hold different authority.
An authenticated request can still carry untrusted data.

topics.title: Control reasoning
details: A threat statement includes asset, actor, action and consequence.
Mitigation must explain how it changes the failure path.

reading.locator: System Modeling, threat identification/ranking, mitigations and review/validation; use the four-question structure for the local notes service.

assignment.title: A trust-boundary diagram with testable controls
instructions: Draw browser, identity verifier, API, database, log sink and backup flows for the fictional service.
Write six threats spanning unauthorized reading, unauthorized modification, data loss and operational misuse.
For each, identify a mechanism and one positive/negative test; document at least one residual risk.
acceptanceCriteria: Client assertions and server-authoritative identity are separated.
Every mitigation explains an enforcement point, not merely a product name.
At least one risk is explicitly accepted or deferred with a reason.

questions.prompt: Does authenticating a user make all their request fields trustworthy?
choices: Yes, all fields become authoritative
No, identity and input validity are separate
Yes, including another user's owner ID
questions.answer: No, identity and input validity are separate
questions.explanation: Authentication identifies a principal; it does not establish that supplied data are valid or that the requested action is authorized.

questions.prompt: What makes 'use encryption' an incomplete mitigation statement?
questions.answer: It does not specify the data state, keys, trust boundary, threat addressed or remaining exposure.
questions.explanation: Mechanisms must be tied to a concrete failure path and verifiable behavior.

reviewPrompts: Where does untrusted data become an authority decision?

lessons.title: Record a minimal baseline and prove restoration
objectives: Inventory software, services and data in a disposable lab.
Verify a baseline backup before changing controls.

topics.title: Attack surface
details: Every service and dependency adds a reason for exposure.
Unused capability is safer removed than merely forgotten.

topics.title: Recovery-first practice
details: A snapshot is useful only if it can be restored and checked.
Lab changes must not alter a shared or production machine.

video.locator: Week 2 Securing Systems: firewalls, antivirus and automatic updates; focus on minimizing exposure and maintaining systems.

reading.locator: Ransomware and Data Extortion Prevention Best Practices: offline backups and tested recovery. Use a harmless synthetic-file loss, never malware.

assignment.title: A restorable local-service baseline
instructions: Inventory the owned lab OS/runtime version, listening service addresses, dependencies and synthetic data locations.
Create a backup or snapshot, change a copied synthetic note and restore the baseline in the isolated environment.
Compare file hashes and application behavior; explicitly state which hardware or network features the lab cannot simulate.
acceptanceCriteria: The service binds only to the declared isolated scope.
Restoration reproduces the known synthetic data and successful application read.
No host firmware, trust store, firewall or real user data is changed.

questions.prompt: What is stronger backup evidence than a successful copy message?
choices: A filename that says backup
A restored copy with verified contents and application use
A large archive size
questions.answer: A restored copy with verified contents and application use
questions.explanation: Recovery depends on readable, complete and usable data, not only the act of copying it.

questions.prompt: Why record limitations of the lab?
questions.answer: They prevent simulated evidence from being misrepresented as proof about hardware, production traffic or controls that were never exercised.
questions.explanation: An honest boundary is part of a credible security assessment.

reviewPrompts: Can the original baseline be restored without relying on undocumented state?

modules.title: 02. Authentication, authorization and sessions
modules.description: Explain how an identity claim becomes a bounded, revocable permission decision.

lessons.title: Explain password verification, MFA and recovery
objectives: Distinguish password hashing from reversible encryption.
Explain authenticator factors, phishing resistance and recovery trade-offs.

topics.title: Verification mechanisms
details: A salted password verifier avoids storing recoverable plaintext.
Work factors and rate limits address different parts of guessing risk.

topics.title: Authenticator lifecycle
details: Two knowledge secrets are not two distinct factors.
Enrollment, device loss and recovery can be weaker than normal login.

video.locator: Week 0 Securing Accounts: authentication, MFA factors, password managers and passkeys. Study defensive mechanisms only.

reading.locator: Authentication Assurance Levels; Authenticator and Verifier Requirements; Authenticator Management. Compare phishing-resistant public-key authenticators with manually entered OTPs.

assignment.title: A synthetic authentication and recovery design
instructions: Use a maintained authentication/password library in the local service with two dummy users and no real passwords.
Verify that equal dummy passwords receive different salts, wrong passwords fail and rate-limit decisions are observable.
Design a factor-loss recovery flow and compare its assurance with the normal sign-in path; do not send messages or collect identity documents.
deliverables: Authentication tests with redacted dummy data
acceptanceCriteria: No plaintext password or reversible password copy is stored or logged.
Factors and recovery paths are distinguished rather than labelled generically MFA.
The design addresses session revocation after an authenticator change.

questions.prompt: Password plus another memorized PIN is best described as what?
choices: Phishing-resistant MFA by definition
Two knowledge secrets, not two distinct factor categories
A hardware possession factor
questions.answer: Two knowledge secrets, not two distinct factor categories
questions.explanation: Factor diversity concerns knowledge, possession and inherence. Adding another memorized secret does not create a possession factor.

questions.prompt: What does a per-user salt protect against, and what does it not do?
questions.answer: It prevents identical passwords from having identical stored verifiers and frustrates reusable precomputed tables; it does not make weak passwords strong or stop all online guessing.
questions.explanation: Salting, password strength, work factors and rate limits address different risks.

reviewPrompts: Can account recovery bypass the strongest login protection?

lessons.title: Enforce least privilege and per-resource authorization
objectives: Express permissions by principal, action, resource and context.
Implement deny-by-default checks independent of UI visibility.

topics.title: Authorization models
details: Roles group privileges; attributes can constrain ownership and context.
A hidden button is not an authorization boundary.

topics.title: Complete mediation
details: Check every relevant server operation, including lists and background jobs.
Use server-established identity rather than trusting a supplied owner field.

video.locator: Week 0 Securing Accounts: authentication versus authorization; use the distinction to explain resource-level checks.

reading.locator: Least Privilege, Deny by Default and Validate the Permissions on Every Request. Translate the principles into a local permission matrix.

assignment.title: A two-owner permission matrix
instructions: Create synthetic users Alice and Bob, each with one note, plus a narrowly scoped support role.
Test read, edit, delete and list operations for owner, other owner, support and anonymous contexts.
Run tests directly against the local server boundary as well as through the UI; use only identifiers from your own fixtures.
acceptanceCriteria: Cross-owner read/write and list leakage are denied.
Missing identity and unknown actions default to deny.
A client-provided owner ID cannot override the authenticated principal.

questions.prompt: Where must a private-note ownership rule be enforced?
choices: Only by hiding an edit button
Only during initial account creation
At the authoritative server/data access boundary for every relevant operation
questions.answer: At the authoritative server/data access boundary for every relevant operation
questions.explanation: Clients can issue requests independently of the interface. Authorization must protect the resource access itself.

questions.prompt: Why test list operations separately from single-record reads?
questions.answer: A list query may omit ownership filtering or leak metadata even when a single-record endpoint checks permissions correctly.
questions.explanation: Each path crossing the trust boundary needs its own evidence.

reviewPrompts: Which operation could reveal another owner's metadata?

lessons.title: Trace session creation, renewal, revocation and federation
objectives: Explain session tokens as temporary bearer authority.
Distinguish authentication federation from access delegation and local authorization.

topics.title: Session lifecycle
details: Rotate identity-bearing sessions at authentication/privilege changes.
Expiration, logout and revocation need authoritative behavior.

topics.title: Federation boundaries
details: An identity provider assertion must have the expected issuer, audience and validity.
OIDC authenticates on top of OAuth; an OAuth access token is not automatically a login identity.

reading.locator: Session ID Properties, Cookies, Session ID Renewal and Session Expiration. Pair with NIST 800-63B-4 Session Management.

assignment.title: A local session lifecycle trace
instructions: Use only dummy local sessions to record pre-login, authenticated, renewed, expired and revoked states.
Test logout and privilege change, including a stale session that must no longer authorize an operation.
Draw a federation message flow and list issuer/audience/expiry checks using invented assertions; do not connect a real provider or capture real tokens.
acceptanceCriteria: Logout or server revocation invalidates the appropriate local session.
Tokens are absent from URLs, logs and submitted evidence.
A valid identity assertion still leads to a separate local authorization decision.

questions.prompt: A validly signed token for a different audience should be what?
choices: Accepted because the signature is valid
Used to skip authorization
Rejected for this service
questions.answer: Rejected for this service
questions.explanation: A signature binds claims to an issuer, but the service must also verify intended audience, validity and other protocol requirements.

questions.prompt: Why does deleting a browser cookie not necessarily revoke the server-side session?
questions.answer: The server may still consider that session valid; authoritative revocation or expiry must govern later requests carrying the old token.
questions.explanation: Client cleanup and server-side authority are different state changes.

reviewPrompts: Where is the final decision that a session is no longer valid?

modules.title: 03. Cryptography, keys and TLS/PKI
modules.description: Explain what each cryptographic mechanism proves and the key/trust assumptions it requires.

lessons.title: Distinguish hashes, MACs, encryption and signatures
objectives: Match confidentiality, integrity and authenticity requirements to primitives.
Use authenticated encryption through a maintained library with safe key/nonce handling.

topics.title: Mechanism roles
details: A hash alone does not authenticate a sender.
A MAC shares a secret; a digital signature uses asymmetric verification.

topics.title: Authenticated encryption
details: AEAD checks integrity as well as confidentiality and can bind associated metadata.
Key/nonce rules and failure handling are part of the security contract.

video.locator: Week 3 Message Integrity 1 and HMAC; Week 4 Authenticated Encryption 1 and 3. Historical examples explain principles, not algorithms to deploy uncritically.

reading.locator: Architectural Design, Algorithms, Cipher Modes and key-management guidance. Never implement your own primitive.

assignment.title: A synthetic authenticated-record envelope
instructions: Use a maintained AEAD library and a disposable generated key to protect two synthetic note records.
Bind an invented record ID as associated data and test successful decryption, changed ciphertext, changed metadata and a wrong key.
Record only test outcomes and key lifecycle decisions, never key bytes; document the library's nonce requirements.
acceptanceCriteria: Tampered ciphertext or associated metadata fails closed.
No unauthenticated partial plaintext is used after verification failure.
Keys are disposable and excluded from source, logs and evidence.

questions.prompt: Which property does a plain hash by itself not provide?
choices: A deterministic digest of the input
A way to compare exact-byte integrity when the expected digest is trusted
Authentication of the sender
questions.answer: Authentication of the sender
questions.explanation: Anyone can compute a hash. Authenticity requires a trusted binding, such as a MAC, signature or independently protected expected digest.

questions.prompt: Why bind a record ID as AEAD associated data?
questions.answer: It lets integrity verification detect ciphertext being presented under the wrong record context, while the associated metadata need not be encrypted.
questions.explanation: Encryption alone does not necessarily bind data to its intended application meaning.

reviewPrompts: What does successful verification prove, and what does it leave unproven?

lessons.title: Explain certificate chains, hostname validation and key lifecycle
objectives: Trace TLS peer authentication and encrypted session establishment.
Test expiry, trust-anchor and hostname failures without disabling verification.

topics.title: PKI
details: A certificate binds a key to an identity under an issuer's policy.
Trust chain, validity and hostname checks solve different problems.

topics.title: TLS boundaries
details: Server-authenticated TLS does not automatically identify the client or authorize an action.
Rotation, revocation and private-key protection remain operational requirements.

video.locator: Week 2 Securing Systems: HTTPS, TLS, X.509 certificates and certificate authorities; separate transport protection from application permission checks.

reading.locator: Server Configuration, Certificates and Client Certificates and Mutual TLS. Use current guidance and per-process lab trust.

assignment.title: Beginner evidence gate: trusted local transport
instructions: Create a disposable local CA/service certificate for a loopback-only lab, trusted only by the test process or disposable VM.
Verify successful connection and explicit rejection of wrong hostname, untrusted issuer and expired certificate fixtures using supported library test facilities.
Submit the threat/permission matrix, session tests and a key-rotation plan; never disable verification or install the CA into the host-wide trust store.
deliverables: TLS trust diagram and positive/negative tests
Integrated identity/transport evidence and cleanup record
acceptanceCriteria: All three invalid-certificate cases fail for the correct reason.
Application authorization is still required after TLS succeeds.
Dummy CA keys and scoped trust are removed from the disposable lab after the exercise.

questions.prompt: A certificate chains to a trusted root but names a different host. What should the client do?
choices: Ignore the name because the chain is valid
Disable verification for all connections
Reject the hostname mismatch
questions.answer: Reject the hostname mismatch
questions.explanation: Trust in an issuer does not make every certificate valid for every service name. Identity matching is a distinct check.

questions.prompt: Why does HTTPS not prove a user may read a particular note?
questions.answer: TLS authenticates/protects the transport endpoint; resource authorization depends on the authenticated application principal and permission policy.
questions.explanation: Cryptographic transport and business authorization enforce different boundaries.

reviewPrompts: Which trust decision happens before the first application request?

modules.title: 04. Operating systems, hardware roots and endpoint controls
modules.description: Trace how privilege, memory isolation, boot trust and patching constrain failures.

lessons.title: Explain process, kernel and mandatory-access boundaries
objectives: Distinguish user/kernel privilege and process memory isolation.
Compare discretionary permissions, capabilities and mandatory access control.

topics.title: OS mediation
details: System calls cross from user code to privileged kernel services.
File ownership and process authority determine permitted operations.

topics.title: Defense in depth
details: MAC policies can constrain an application beyond ordinary user permissions.
Memory protections reduce classes of failure but are not proof of bug-free code.

reading.locator: Linux Security Module Usage: enforcement hooks, MAC examples, capabilities and active-module inspection. Treat exact configuration as version-specific.

assignment.title: A least-privilege file-access experiment
instructions: Inside an owned disposable Linux VM/container, create separate synthetic service and reviewer accounts with one private test file.
Record allowed and denied read/write operations under normal permissions; inspect available MAC controls without disabling them.
Draw the kernel mediation path and explain ASLR, non-executable memory and memory-safe language benefits conceptually, without exploitation.
acceptanceCriteria: The service cannot write reviewer-only synthetic data.
Tests run in the declared disposable scope, not on real user directories.
The explanation distinguishes permission enforcement from memory-corruption mitigations.

questions.prompt: Which component ultimately mediates a local file-open permission check?
choices: Only the application's button label
The operating system kernel and configured security controls
The filename's appearance
questions.answer: The operating system kernel and configured security controls
questions.explanation: Applications request operations; kernel and security policy enforce the authority boundary. Application checks can add further constraints.

questions.prompt: Why is running a service with minimal privilege valuable even if its code is intended to be correct?
questions.answer: If the service is misused or contains a defect, reduced authority limits the resources and operations it can affect.
questions.explanation: Least privilege reduces consequences; it does not eliminate the need to fix defects.

reviewPrompts: What authority does the process actually need?

lessons.title: Trace secure boot, measurement, TPM and disk encryption
objectives: Distinguish prevention by verified boot from evidence by measured boot.
Explain how disk encryption and hardware-bound keys protect specific data states.

topics.title: Boot trust
details: Secure Boot checks allowed signed components in a chain.
Measured Boot records measurements that can inform attestation or key release.

topics.title: At-rest limits
details: A TPM can protect/seal keys to conditions; it is not a general guarantee of clean software.
Full-disk encryption protects a powered-off disk differently from a logged-in compromised process.

video.locator: Week 4 Odds and Ends 3: disk encryption and creditcard encryption. Focus on at-rest threat boundaries; use current platform documentation for actual settings.

reading.locator: Secure Boot, Trusted Boot and Measured Boot sections; distinguish signature enforcement, measurement and attestation.

assignment.title: A boot-to-data protection map
instructions: Draw firmware, bootloader, kernel, TPM-bound key and encrypted volume trust relationships from the official documentation.
Evaluate stolen powered-off disk, unlocked running session and unexpected boot measurement scenarios.

Inspect only read-only status inside a supported disposable lab if available; otherwise label the exercise a documentation-backed design. Never change firmware keys, host encryption or recovery settings.
acceptanceCriteria: Secure and measured boot are not treated as identical.
Disk encryption is not claimed to stop an authorized running process reading plaintext.
Recovery-key availability and protection are part of the design.

questions.prompt: What does full-disk encryption most directly protect?
choices: Data on storage when the decryption key is unavailable
Every action of an already authorized running process
All network traffic automatically
questions.answer: Data on storage when the decryption key is unavailable
questions.explanation: Once a system has unlocked the data for use, process and application permissions still matter.

questions.prompt: How does measured boot differ from secure boot?
questions.answer: Measured boot records component measurements for evaluation/attestation; secure boot enforces a policy about which signed boot components may execute.
questions.explanation: Evidence about a state and prevention of an unapproved state are related but distinct mechanisms.

reviewPrompts: What happens if the recovery key is unavailable or exposed?

lessons.title: Operate patching, endpoint policy and rollback safely
objectives: Connect asset inventory to supported software and update decisions.
Test a controlled update without treating detection tools as infallible.

topics.title: Endpoint layers
details: Updates remove known defects; endpoint controls observe or block classes of behavior.
Application allowlisting and least privilege can reduce unnecessary execution.

topics.title: Change governance
details: Patch urgency, compatibility and rollback all need evidence.
A disabled alert or unsupported OS should not silently become the baseline.

video.locator: Week 2 Securing Systems: antivirus and automatic updates. Explain why these complement rather than replace permissions and backups.

reading.locator: Prevention best practices: asset management, patching, least privilege and backups. Avoid any offensive examples; use a benign local dependency update.

assignment.title: A reversible endpoint maintenance record
instructions: Select one benign lab runtime/dependency update using its official release/security information and the baseline inventory.
Back up, update only the disposable lab and run service, permission and recovery checks.
Document a rollback rehearsal or a safely simulated incompatibility; do not disable host protections or deploy a known vulnerable target.
acceptanceCriteria: The changed component and source are identifiable.
Core service and least-privilege checks remain valid after the update.
Failed validation triggers an explicit pause or rollback rather than being marked successful.

questions.prompt: Which is an adequate patch-completion claim?
choices: The download finished
The intended version is installed and relevant behavior/control checks pass
Alerts were disabled so no errors appeared
questions.answer: The intended version is installed and relevant behavior/control checks pass
questions.explanation: Installation and functional/security verification are distinct. Suppressing alerts is not remediation evidence.

questions.prompt: Why retain the pre-update baseline?
questions.answer: It supports comparison, diagnosis and controlled rollback when a change breaks functionality or a security assumption.
questions.explanation: A recoverable change is safer than an undocumented irreversible one.

reviewPrompts: Which observable result proves the update took effect?

modules.title: 05. Networking, segmentation and detection
modules.description: Explain packet routing and control placement, including what encryption hides from sensors.

lessons.title: Trace TCP, DNS and a service boundary
objectives: Explain address, port, transport connection and name resolution roles.
Distinguish DNS authenticity, DNS privacy and application TLS.

topics.title: Network mechanics
details: IP routes packets; transport ports identify service endpoints.
A connection to an address is not proof of application identity.

topics.title: DNS
details: Recursive resolvers and authoritative servers have different responsibilities.
DNSSEC authenticates supported DNS data; encrypted DNS protects a transport link, and neither replaces application authorization.

video.locator: Week 2 Securing Systems: IP addresses, ports, HTTPS and proxies. Restrict any observation to self-generated local traffic.

reading.locator: RFC 1034 Sections 3 Domain Name Space and Resource Records, 4 Name Servers and 5 Resolvers, especially caching. Pair with RFC 4033 Sections 3-4 for DNSSEC's service and limitation boundaries.

assignment.title: A local name-to-service trace
instructions: Use a reserved synthetic hostname and a loopback service, or an isolated host-only resolver with locally authored records.
Record lookup result, address/port and TLS/application identity checks as separate steps; capture only your own benign lab traffic if capture is used.
Diagram a client, application and database segment with required flows and explicitly denied direct database access.
acceptanceCriteria: Name resolution is not confused with user authentication.
No real-user traffic or public network is scanned/captured.
The database is reachable only through a justified lab flow.

questions.prompt: What does a DNS answer primarily provide to a client?
choices: Name-related records such as an address
Permission to read every application record
A guarantee that the user is authenticated
questions.answer: Name-related records such as an address
questions.explanation: Resolution is one step before connecting. TLS identity and application access decisions remain separate.

questions.prompt: Why are DNSSEC and encrypted DNS not the same protection?
questions.answer: DNSSEC validates signed DNS data where deployed; encrypted DNS protects the client-resolver transport from some observers, with a different trust boundary.
questions.explanation: Integrity/authenticity of records and privacy of a transport link solve different problems.

reviewPrompts: Which device knows the hostname, and which knows the application identity?

lessons.title: Place firewall and VPN controls at the right boundary
objectives: Explain stateful filtering and default-deny flow policy.
Identify where a VPN's protection ends and application controls begin.

topics.title: Firewall policy
details: Rules match declared traffic properties at a specific enforcement point.
State tracking does not understand every business authorization rule.

topics.title: VPN trust
details: A VPN encrypts a tunnel between endpoints, not every remaining path.
Network location alone should not grant broad application authority.

video.locator: Week 2 Securing Systems: VPN, firewall and HTTPS. Identify tunnel endpoints and the continuing need for application TLS.

reading.locator: Publication overview and full publication sections Firewall Technologies and Firewall Policy. Use the 2009 document for architecture principles, not current vendor commands.

assignment.title: An isolated segmentation policy
instructions: In a disposable VM/network namespace only, permit a test client to the app and the app to its test database, denying other flows.
Verify allowed/denied flows with harmless connection attempts to those explicitly owned endpoints.
Overlay a hypothetical VPN tunnel and explain which traffic remains outside it; provide a rollback procedure before applying rules.
acceptanceCriteria: Rules implement the declared flow matrix and preserve needed management access in the lab.
Tests do not touch the host firewall or external networks.
The explanation does not equate VPN access with record-level permission.

questions.prompt: A VPN connection to a private network should automatically grant what application privileges?
choices: Administrative access to every service
None beyond separately evaluated identity and policy
Access to every user's records
questions.answer: None beyond separately evaluated identity and policy
questions.explanation: A tunnel protects transport to its endpoint. It is not a universal application authorization decision.

questions.prompt: Why keep a rollback path for a firewall change?
questions.answer: An incorrect rule can cut off legitimate service or management access; rollback preserves availability while the error is diagnosed.
questions.explanation: Security controls must be introduced with operational recovery, not simply enabled and assumed correct.

reviewPrompts: Which request must still be rejected after the network permits the connection?

lessons.title: Explain IDS/IPS visibility and detection trade-offs
objectives: Read a signature's action, scope and matching conditions.
Measure true/false alerts on benign labelled local fixtures.

topics.title: Sensor roles
details: IDS alerts; inline IPS may block under a configured policy.
Encrypted payloads reduce network visibility, so endpoint/application telemetry remains important.

topics.title: Detection quality
details: A match is evidence for investigation, not proof of compromise.
False positives and false negatives require labelled evaluation.

reading.locator: Rules Format: Action, Header, Protocol and Rule Options. Use a harmless training marker instead of attack signatures or payloads.

assignment.title: A benign training-marker detector
instructions: Generate a small set of owned local HTTP health-check requests containing or omitting the literal marker training-demo.
Use an offline capture from only this lab or a synthetic rule-evaluation table to predict and verify alerts; state honestly which mode was executed.
Label expected matches, compute false positives/negatives and explain why TLS payload encryption changes sensor coverage without teaching bypass.
deliverables: Rule interpretation and labelled benign fixture
acceptanceCriteria: Every alert maps to an expected condition or a documented false positive.
The exercise uses no attack payload, evasion, third-party capture or public probing.
The report distinguishes alerting from prevention and from confirmed incident evidence.

questions.prompt: An IDS alert proves which statement?
choices: A compromise definitely occurred
The traffic was necessarily blocked
A configured detection condition matched observed data
questions.answer: A configured detection condition matched observed data
questions.explanation: Alerts require context and triage. IDS and IPS enforcement behavior also differ.

questions.prompt: Why retain application logs when using a network sensor?
questions.answer: Application logs can reveal authenticated actions and resource context that a network sensor may not see, especially with encrypted payloads.
questions.explanation: Different telemetry layers observe different parts of the trust boundary.

reviewPrompts: What exactly can this sensor observe, and what can it not conclude?

modules.title: 06. Application, API and database protections
modules.description: Treat parsing, authorization, query construction and data permissions as separate enforcement mechanisms.

lessons.title: Keep input data separate from executable instructions
objectives: Explain server-side validation, parameterized queries and contextual output encoding.
Test the local API's types, sizes and response behavior with harmless malformed data.

topics.title: Input boundaries
details: Validation enforces shape/range; authorization enforces who may act.
Parameterized queries separate data from query syntax.

topics.title: Output boundaries
details: HTML, URL and other output contexts need appropriate encoding.
Errors should be useful without disclosing secrets or internals.

video.locator: Week 3 Securing Software: prepared statements, client/server validation and character escapes. Practice only defensive cases in the owned service.

reading.locator: Input Validation, Validate Content Types, Access Control and Error Handling. Verify that parsing and permission checks serve different purposes.

assignment.title: A defensive API contract suite
instructions: Test valid note creation, oversized text, wrong JSON types, missing identity and unsupported content type against the local fixture service.
Use parameter binding for a dummy note containing ordinary quotes and markup-like text; render it as text rather than instructions.
Record expected status codes and sanitized errors without generating exploit payloads or targeting any other application.
acceptanceCriteria: Invalid data never reaches a database mutation.
User text remains data in both query and display contexts.
Errors and test artifacts expose no credentials or private environment details.

questions.prompt: Why use a parameterized query for user-supplied text?
choices: To keep the text in the data channel rather than query syntax
To grant the user more permissions
To encrypt the whole database automatically
questions.answer: To keep the text in the data channel rather than query syntax
questions.explanation: Parameter binding addresses interpretation at the query boundary. Authorization and encryption remain separate controls.

questions.prompt: Why is client-side validation alone insufficient?
questions.answer: The authoritative service can receive requests that do not originate from that client interface, so it must validate its own inputs.
questions.explanation: The server cannot delegate trust enforcement to untrusted callers.

reviewPrompts: Which protection changes interpretation, and which changes permission?

lessons.title: Enforce database privilege and recoverable data integrity
objectives: Separate application, migration and backup privileges.
Test owner-scoped data access and transaction rollback.

topics.title: Data authority
details: Database authentication does not imply unrestricted table access.
Row ownership and service-level authorization must agree.

topics.title: Integrity and recovery
details: Transactions prevent partial multi-step changes under a stated isolation model.
A backup needs both access control and verified restoration.

reading.locator: PostgreSQL manual: Database Roles, Privileges and Row Security Policies. Use a local disposable database with synthetic rows; distinguish role grants from application ownership.

assignment.title: Intermediate evidence gate: a bounded data service
instructions: Give the synthetic application a limited database role separate from schema migration and backup roles.
Verify owner-scoped reads/writes and a transaction that rolls back after an intentional harmless validation failure.
Restore a synthetic backup in the isolated lab and attach the OS, firewall and benign IDS evidence from this stage.
deliverables: Role/row permission tests and rollback trace
Restored-service check and stage control map
acceptanceCriteria: The application role cannot perform schema administration.
A failed transaction leaves no partial synthetic update.
Cross-owner data remain inaccessible and restored data match the baseline.
Network and endpoint control evidence states exactly which layers were tested.

questions.prompt: Why separate the migration role from the normal application role?
choices: It automatically removes all bugs
It makes backups unnecessary
Routine requests should not have schema-changing authority
questions.answer: Routine requests should not have schema-changing authority
questions.explanation: Separate privileges reduce the impact of application defects or misuse and make sensitive operations auditable.

questions.prompt: What should a transaction rollback test verify beyond receiving an error?
questions.answer: It should inspect persistent state to confirm that none of the intended atomic changes were partially committed.
questions.explanation: An error response does not by itself prove data integrity.

reviewPrompts: Which layer enforces ownership if the application query is wrong?

modules.title: 07. Browser/API boundaries and verification evidence
modules.description: Reason about cookies, cross-origin behavior, tokens and multi-tenant ownership, then verify against a scoped standard.

lessons.title: Explain cookies, CSRF defenses, CORS and security headers
objectives: Distinguish browser-enforced policies from server authorization.
Verify session cookie and state-changing request safeguards.

topics.title: Browser context
details: Cookies can be attached automatically to eligible requests.
SameSite, Secure and HttpOnly constrain different behaviors.

topics.title: Cross-origin controls
details: CORS governs browser response sharing, not general API authorization.
CSRF defenses protect state changes; output encoding and CSP address other boundaries.

video.locator: MIT 6.858 Lecture 9: Securing Web Applications. Use historical architecture principles, checking current browser behavior against OWASP rather than adopting old defaults.

reading.locator: Cookies: Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite attributes; Session Management WAF Protections and lifecycle guidance. Pair with REST guidance on security headers.

assignment.title: A local browser-boundary verification
instructions: Inspect only your lab's dummy session cookie attributes and explain each flag's function.
Use owned local test origins to verify allowed/disallowed response sharing and server-side permission checks independently.
Test a state-changing request with missing/incorrect CSRF context where cookie sessions require that defense; use benign note updates, not payloads.
acceptanceCriteria: CORS denial is not used as a replacement for server authorization.
Cookie flags are justified separately and tokens never enter the report.
State-changing requests require the appropriate server-validated anti-CSRF or protocol control.

questions.prompt: Can CORS alone protect an API from unauthorized non-browser requests?
choices: No, the API still needs server-side authentication and authorization
Yes, all clients obey browser CORS rules
Yes, if the header is hidden
questions.answer: No, the API still needs server-side authentication and authorization
questions.explanation: CORS is a browser response-sharing policy. It does not establish the caller's permission at the service boundary.

questions.prompt: How do HttpOnly and Secure differ?
questions.answer: HttpOnly limits script access to a cookie; Secure limits sending it to secure transport contexts under browser rules.
questions.explanation: Neither flag alone solves every session, CSRF or application authorization risk.

reviewPrompts: Which protections still apply to a non-browser caller?

lessons.title: Test multi-tenant access and background authority
objectives: Verify resource ownership across reads, lists, writes and asynchronous work.
Prevent stale or changed identity from leaking another synthetic tenant's data.

topics.title: Tenant isolation
details: Object IDs identify resources but do not grant access.
Caches, queues and exports must preserve the same tenant boundary.

topics.title: Identity transitions
details: A background operation must retain the correct initiating scope.
Account switching must not expose the previous owner's private state.

reading.locator: Validate Permissions on Every Request, attribute/relationship-based controls and authorization tests. Apply them beyond normal UI reads.

assignment.title: An owner-boundary regression matrix
instructions: Using only Alice/Bob synthetic fixtures, test direct reads, lists, edits, exports and one queued task for each owner.
Switch local identities while a delayed read is pending and ensure the previous result is not displayed or written under the new owner.
Record permission decisions and redacted tenant IDs, including anonymous and stale-session cases.
acceptanceCriteria: Every cross-owner access is denied without leaking content or private metadata.
Queued/cached data remain bound to their original authorized scope.
Denied operations have visible, non-sensitive error records.

questions.prompt: Knowing another synthetic tenant's object ID should grant what?
choices: Read access by default
No access without an independent permission check
Permission to export the tenant
questions.answer: No access without an independent permission check
questions.explanation: Identifiers locate resources. Authorization determines whether a principal may act on them.

questions.prompt: Why test a delayed response during account switching?
questions.answer: A response authorized for the previous identity can arrive after the interface has changed owners, exposing or corrupting data if identity generation is not checked.
questions.explanation: Access control includes lifecycle and asynchronous state, not only a synchronous endpoint check.

reviewPrompts: Where might an owner ID be lost between components?

lessons.title: Turn ASVS requirements into scoped verification evidence
objectives: Select relevant verification requirements without claiming full compliance.
Record pass, fail and not-applicable decisions with reproducible evidence.

topics.title: Assurance scope
details: A standard provides requirements, not automatic protection.
Version and applicability decisions must accompany a checklist.

topics.title: Evidence quality
details: A screenshot is weaker than a reproducible permission/validation test.
A not-applicable decision needs a threat-model-based reason.

reading.locator: Use the existing hosted ASVS 5.0.0 PDF: locate Authentication, Session Management, Authorization, and API/Web Service requirements. Record exact versioned requirement IDs from the PDF, not older ASVS numbering.

assignment.title: A scoped ASVS verification matrix
instructions: Select at least eight relevant ASVS 5.0.0 requirements spanning identity, sessions, authorization, data and API boundaries.
For each, record the exact ID, applicability, implementation mechanism, test command and evidence.
Keep at least one real lab gap visible with remediation and owner; do not label the service certified or wholly ASVS-compliant.
acceptanceCriteria: All selected IDs are verified against the existing 5.0.0 artifact.
Pass entries have repeatable evidence and not-applicable entries have reasons.
The conclusion states the limited sample and unresolved issues.

questions.prompt: Passing eight selected requirements supports which claim?
choices: Those scoped requirements were checked with the recorded evidence
The selected sample establishes the entire ASVS verification level
The service no longer needs threat-model review after feature changes
questions.answer: Those scoped requirements were checked with the recorded evidence
questions.explanation: Assurance is bounded by requirements, scope, version and test coverage. A sample is not an independent certification.

questions.prompt: What should justify a not-applicable result?
questions.answer: A documented architectural or threat-model reason showing why the requirement's relevant capability or exposure is absent.
questions.explanation: Not applicable is an evidence-backed scope decision, not a convenient substitute for an unimplemented control.

reviewPrompts: Which requirement has the weakest evidence rather than the most polished description?

modules.title: 08. Cloud IAM, secrets and software supply chain
modules.description: Explain authority and artifact trust without deploying a cloud account or handling real secrets.

lessons.title: Reason about cloud identities and effective permissions
objectives: Distinguish identity policy, resource policy, permissions boundary and explicit deny.
Explain workload identity and shared responsibility.

topics.title: Effective authority
details: Policy interactions depend on principal and resource context.
Explicit deny overrides allows in the documented evaluation model.

topics.title: Cloud boundaries
details: Provider infrastructure controls do not replace customer identity/data configuration.
Short-lived workload credentials reduce exposure compared with unmanaged static keys.

reading.locator: Evaluating identity-based policies with resource-based policies; permissions boundaries; Organizations SCPs. Read the linked caveats before generalizing a simplified exercise.

assignment.title: An offline IAM policy decision table
instructions: Create six fictitious same-account requests for a role, initially with identity policies only and no resource-policy grants.
Evaluate explicit deny, missing allow and a permissions boundary; then describe how adding a resource policy requires revisiting the model.
Assign provider/customer responsibilities for patching, data encryption configuration and access review. Do not provision or modify any cloud resource.
acceptanceCriteria: An explicit deny is never overridden by a more permissive allow in the exercise.
A boundary is not treated as an independent grant.
The simplified table is not described as a complete AWS evaluator or a cloud compliance proof.

questions.prompt: In the documented IAM model, what does an applicable explicit deny do?
choices: Overrides an allow
Is overridden by a broader allow attached to the same principal
Applies only before the principal successfully authenticates
questions.answer: Overrides an allow
questions.explanation: Authentication establishes identity; applicable policy evaluation, including explicit deny, determines effective authority.

questions.prompt: Why does a permissions boundary not grant an action on its own?
questions.answer: It constrains the maximum identity-based permissions; an applicable grant is still required under the relevant evaluation rules.
questions.explanation: A limit on authority is distinct from a source of authority.

reviewPrompts: Which policy grants authority, and which only limits it?

lessons.title: Design secret issuance, rotation, revocation and key recovery
objectives: Map secret/key access through creation, storage, use and retirement.
Rotate dummy credentials without logging them or silently accepting old authority.

topics.title: Secret lifecycle
details: A secret store needs its own access and availability policy.
Versioning supports rotation, but old credentials need a retirement decision.

topics.title: Key management
details: Envelope encryption separates data keys from key-encryption keys.
Key loss affects availability; key compromise affects confidentiality and trust.

video.locator: Week 4 Odds and Ends 1: how to derive keys; Week 5 Basic Key Exchange 1. Distinguish cryptographic key establishment from operational secret distribution.

reading.locator: General Secrets Management: least privilege, lifecycle, rotation and auditing. Pair with Cryptographic Storage guidance on key handling.

assignment.title: A dummy-secret rotation and revocation drill
instructions: Use generated disposable dummy credentials in the local fixture service, referenced by version/handle rather than embedded in code.
Rotate to a new version, verify intended clients continue, then revoke the old version and test rejection.
Simulate secret-store unavailability and key-loss recovery using only synthetic copies; capture outcomes, never values.
deliverables: Rotation, revocation and outage test log
acceptanceCriteria: No secret value appears in source, logs, screenshots or evidence.
The revoked version cannot authorize a new request.
Outage behavior is explicit and fail-closed for protected operations; recovery is tested.

questions.prompt: A credential is rotated but the old value remains valid indefinitely. What is still missing?
choices: A controlled retirement/revocation policy
A second issued value without an expiry for the first
A rotation log message without testing old-client access
questions.answer: A controlled retirement/revocation policy
questions.explanation: Creating a new secret does not remove authority from the old one. Rotation includes transition and retirement.

questions.prompt: Why separate data keys from key-encryption keys?
questions.answer: It supports scoped data encryption and managed wrapping/rotation boundaries, while concentrating protection requirements on the higher-level keys.
questions.explanation: The hierarchy improves manageability but still requires correct access controls, backup and lifecycle handling.

reviewPrompts: Who can use, rotate, revoke and recover each secret?

lessons.title: Verify dependencies, build provenance and release artifacts
objectives: Distinguish hashes, signatures, provenance and vulnerability information.
Design least-privilege build and dependency-update gates.

topics.title: Artifact trust
details: A checksum identifies bytes; a signature binds a signer under a trust policy.
Provenance links inputs and build process, not automatic code safety.

topics.title: Delivery controls
details: Pin dependencies and review updates using supported versions.
CI permissions, third-party actions and secret exposure affect the build boundary.

video.locator: Week 3 Securing Software: package managers, updates, CVE and vulnerability prioritization. Treat advisories as inputs to triage, not proof of exploitation.

reading.locator: Build track and Build L1/L2/L3 descriptions: distinguish provenance existence, signed hosted-build provenance and hardened build guarantees.

assignment.title: A local release provenance pack
instructions: Inventory dependencies/licenses in the synthetic service and generate a simple SBOM/manifest with exact versions and artifact hashes.
Build from a clean local environment and compare a modified copy against the expected hash; do not publish a malicious package or alter external registries.
Design a CI permission and review policy, marking which SLSA properties are demonstrated and which are only proposed.
deliverables: Artifact verification and CI authority review
acceptanceCriteria: A changed artifact fails identity verification.
The build record identifies source revision, inputs and process.
No SLSA level or vulnerability-free claim is inferred from a manifest alone.

questions.prompt: Matching an artifact's expected hash establishes what?
choices: Byte identity with the trusted expected digest
That the code has no vulnerabilities
That the author is automatically trustworthy
questions.answer: Byte identity with the trusted expected digest
questions.explanation: The expected hash must itself be obtained through a trusted channel. Byte identity is not a security review of the content.

questions.prompt: Why restrict CI token permissions even for a private repository?
questions.answer: Build steps and dependencies can be compromised or misconfigured; limiting token authority reduces the impact on code, releases and secrets.
questions.explanation: Build infrastructure is another trust boundary, not inherently safe because it is internal.

reviewPrompts: What evidence connects this binary to the reviewed source?

modules.title: 09. Security telemetry and detection engineering
modules.description: Create evidence that supports triage while minimizing private data and alert noise.

lessons.title: Design structured, privacy-preserving security events
objectives: Record actor, action, result, resource and correlation context.
Protect log integrity, retention and sensitive-data boundaries.

topics.title: Event design
details: Event time and ingest time support ordering and delay analysis.
Correlation IDs link events without copying credentials or full payloads.

topics.title: Log trust
details: Restricted writers/readers and external copies improve tamper resistance.
An application-generated log is evidence with limitations, not absolute non-repudiation.

reading.locator: Event Attributes, Data to Exclude, Verification and Protection. Define a bounded schema and test it with synthetic entries.

assignment.title: A redacted event contract
instructions: Generate synthetic login outcome, denied note access, role change, secret rotation and restore events.
Validate event/ingest timestamps, actor pseudonyms, action, outcome and correlation IDs; exclude passwords, tokens and full note bodies.
Test access restrictions and a log-sink outage, including how dropped events are surfaced rather than silently ignored.
acceptanceCriteria: Every event has sufficient context to distinguish a denied action from success.
No credential or sensitive payload enters stored/logged output.
Logging failure produces a visible operational signal under a documented policy.

questions.prompt: Which belongs in a security log?
choices: A plaintext password
A pseudonymous actor, action, outcome and correlation ID
A reusable session token
questions.answer: A pseudonymous actor, action, outcome and correlation ID
questions.explanation: Logs need investigative context, not reusable secrets. Data minimization reduces the harm if a log store is exposed.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish event time from ingest time?
questions.answer: Delayed collection and clock differences can otherwise distort an incident timeline or hide telemetry outages.
questions.explanation: A trustworthy chronology records both when something happened and when it became visible to the monitoring system.

reviewPrompts: Could this log help an investigator without exposing the underlying private content?

lessons.title: Evaluate detections with labelled synthetic cases
objectives: Translate a threat hypothesis into observable conditions and triage steps.
Measure false positives, false negatives and missing visibility.

topics.title: Detection contracts
details: A rule needs a data source, threshold/window and response owner.
Thresholds can hide rare events or overwhelm operators.

topics.title: Coverage
details: No alert is not proof of no incident.
Evaluate both benign and concerning synthetic sequences.

reading.locator: Chapter 6 Monitoring Distributed Systems: symptoms, actionable alerts and avoiding excessive noise. Pair with OWASP Logging verification guidance.

assignment.title: Advanced evidence gate: a labelled detection pack
instructions: Create labelled synthetic sequences for repeated denied access, an approved role change, an unapproved role change and a missing log interval.
Implement bounded-window rules and evaluate them on a separate fixture set; include a benign sequence likely to trigger a naive rule.
Link detections to the threat/ASVS matrix, offline IAM decisions, secret rotation and supply-chain evidence from this stage.
deliverables: Triage playbooks and stage coverage/gap map
acceptanceCriteria: Expected positives and negatives are evaluated, not only matched examples.
At least one false positive or visibility gap is documented and addressed or accepted.
Alerts contain an owner, reason and safe next investigative step.

questions.prompt: A fixture has 10 truly concerning sequences and the rule detects 8. How many false negatives remain?
questions.explanation: Ten actual positives minus eight detected positives leaves two missed cases. Their mechanisms matter as much as the count.

questions.prompt: Why evaluate a benign approved role change?
questions.answer: It tests whether the rule can distinguish authorized maintenance from a concerning change and whether it would create avoidable operator noise.
questions.explanation: Detection usefulness depends on discrimination and triage context, not just the ability to emit alerts.

reviewPrompts: What could happen without producing any event this rule can observe?

modules.title: 10. Incident response, backups and recovery
modules.description: Use harmless incident fixtures to practice containment, evidence handling and verifiable restoration.

lessons.title: Triage and contain a synthetic incident
objectives: Separate observed facts, hypotheses and scope uncertainty.
Choose reversible containment while preserving evidence.

topics.title: Incident reasoning
details: An alert needs validation and business-impact assessment.
Evidence handling records source, time, handler and integrity checks.

topics.title: Containment
details: Revoke a dummy session or isolate a lab component instead of destroying data.
Containment and root-cause analysis have different immediate goals.

reading.locator: SP 800-61 Rev. 3 publication overview and linked full text: CSF 2.0 Detect and Respond recommendations. Focus on analysis, incident scope, communication and mitigation.

assignment.title: An evidence-preserving tabletop incident
instructions: Use a prepared synthetic alert showing an unexpected privilege change and a dummy session still active after revocation.
Build a timeline with facts, hypotheses, affected assets and confidence; hash copied evidence and record its handling.
Contain only the disposable lab identity/component, preserving original fixtures and documenting expected user impact.
acceptanceCriteria: Facts are distinguished from unconfirmed hypotheses.
Evidence copies and handling are traceable without real sensitive data.
Containment is scoped, reversible where possible and checked for effectiveness.

questions.prompt: What should happen before treating an alert's interpretation as fact?
choices: Assume the alert's severity also establishes the affected scope
Contain all connected systems before checking authorization and impact
Validate the observation and preserve evidence with uncertainty stated
questions.answer: Validate the observation and preserve evidence with uncertainty stated
questions.explanation: An alert is a signal, not a complete incident narrative. Validation and evidence preservation support a defensible response.

questions.prompt: Why can immediate deletion be a poor containment action?
questions.answer: It can destroy evidence, prevent diagnosis and disrupt recovery without actually removing the underlying access path.
questions.explanation: Containment should reduce ongoing impact while preserving the information needed for investigation and restoration.

reviewPrompts: Which containment action changes the least while reducing the immediate risk?

lessons.title: Test backup isolation, RPO and RTO
objectives: Define acceptable data loss and recovery time as separate objectives.
Restore verified synthetic data and recheck access controls.

topics.title: Backup design
details: A replica can replicate unwanted changes; versioned/offline backups serve a different role.
Restore keys and permissions are part of recoverability.

topics.title: Recovery evidence
details: RPO concerns the recoverable data point; RTO concerns time to restore service.
A service that starts with incorrect ownership or missing data is not fully recovered.

reading.locator: Prevention guidance on offline/encrypted backups and the response checklist's recovery actions. Test restoration with benign synthetic copies only.

assignment.title: A timed, harmless restore drill
instructions: Set an invented RPO of one hour and RTO of 30 minutes for the small isolated service.
Use a prepared copy with missing synthetic records to simulate data loss; restore from a known-good backup without running malware or altering original user data.
Measure recovery duration, latest recovered event and owner-permission tests; report misses honestly rather than changing targets after the drill.
acceptanceCriteria: Recovered data and record counts match the declared backup point.
Measured data loss and service recovery time are reported separately.
Authentication, authorization and logging remain effective after restoration.

questions.prompt: Which objective concerns how much recent data might be lost?
choices: RPO
RTO
Password length
questions.answer: RPO
questions.explanation: Recovery Point Objective limits the acceptable data gap; Recovery Time Objective limits the duration to restore the required service.

questions.prompt: Why is a live replica not a complete backup strategy?
questions.answer: It may quickly reproduce deletion, corruption or unauthorized changes, leaving no intact earlier version to recover.
questions.explanation: Versioning, isolation and tested restoration address failure modes that availability replicas alone do not.

reviewPrompts: Was the service merely running, or was its security state also restored?

lessons.title: Coordinate response roles and a blameless improvement review
objectives: Assign incident command, technical, communication and approval responsibilities.
Translate findings into verified corrective actions.

topics.title: Coordination
details: Status updates should distinguish impact, uncertainty and next actions.
Notification obligations depend on actual jurisdiction and contracts.

topics.title: Learning
details: A post-incident review examines system conditions, not just individual blame.
Each corrective action needs an owner and verification evidence.

reading.locator: Rev. 3 CSF-aligned Respond and Recover recommendations: incident communication, coordination and improvement. Consult current applicable authorities for any real reporting obligation.

assignment.title: A synthetic incident tabletop and postmortem
instructions: Run a timed tabletop with scripted injects: alert uncertainty, backup mismatch and a service-owner request to resume early.
Record who decides containment, communicates status and approves recovery; a solo learner can role-play these as separate written passes.
Write a no-blame postmortem with three prioritized actions and proof required to close each.
acceptanceCriteria: Uncertainty and impact remain explicit in status updates.
Recovery approval waits for stated checks, not pressure alone.
No invented legal deadline or notification to real third parties is performed.

questions.prompt: Which corrective action is most auditable?
choices: Ask the on-call team to remember the issue without a check or owner
Close the incident on service recovery without tracking prevention work
Add and demonstrate a stale-session revocation regression test with an owner and deadline
questions.answer: Add and demonstrate a stale-session revocation regression test with an owner and deadline
questions.explanation: A concrete owner, change and verification criterion can be tracked to closure. Vague intentions cannot.

questions.prompt: Why separate incident communication from speculative attribution?
questions.answer: Stakeholders need reliable impact and response information, while attribution may remain uncertain and premature claims can mislead or harm.
questions.explanation: Evidence-led communication supports response without converting hypotheses into public accusations.

reviewPrompts: Which action reduces recurrence and how will you know it worked?

modules.title: 11. Risk governance and security architecture
modules.description: Connect mechanism-level evidence to business outcomes, residual risk and sustainable operations.

lessons.title: Build a CSF profile and accountable risk register
objectives: Map controls and gaps to Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
Record risk ownership, treatment and expiring exceptions.

topics.title: Risk decisions
details: Risk combines plausible impact with likelihood/uncertainty, not just a tool's score.
Acceptance is an accountable decision, not the absence of a fix.

topics.title: Profiles
details: Current and target profiles describe outcomes and priorities.
Framework alignment is not a certification or proof of compliance.

reading.locator: CSF 2.0 Core and Organizational Profiles/quick-start material linked from the official hub; cover all six functions, including Govern.

assignment.title: A scoped security risk and exception register
instructions: Map the lab's implemented controls and open gaps to the six CSF functions.
Prioritize five risks by documented impact and uncertainty, assigning an owner, treatment and evidence needed for closure.
Create one time-limited exception with compensating controls and a review/expiry condition.
acceptanceCriteria: All six functions have relevant outcomes or justified scope notes.
Risk acceptance has an owner and rationale rather than a silent default.
Exceptions expire and include measurable compensating checks.

questions.prompt: An accepted risk should have what?
choices: The scanner's default score without an accountable acceptance decision
A permanent exception that needs no review while the service stays online
An accountable owner, rationale and review conditions
questions.answer: An accountable owner, rationale and review conditions
questions.explanation: Acceptance does not remove the exposure. It records who understands and takes responsibility for a bounded decision.

questions.prompt: Why include Govern in addition to technical controls?
questions.answer: Authority, policy, responsibilities and risk decisions determine which controls are sustained, reviewed and corrected over time.
questions.explanation: Technical mechanisms depend on organizational ownership and decision processes.

reviewPrompts: Who can knowingly accept this risk, and for how long?

lessons.title: Design a resource-centered, defense-in-depth architecture
objectives: Explain policy decision/enforcement points and continuous context checks.
Compare centralized and distributed controls with availability and privacy trade-offs.

topics.title: Zero trust principles
details: Network location does not automatically establish trust.
Access decisions are scoped to resources, identity and current context.

topics.title: Architecture trade-offs
details: Central policy improves consistency but creates availability/dependency concerns.
Telemetry and repeated checks must minimize unnecessary personal data.

reading.locator: Linked SP 800-207 full publication: Tenets of Zero Trust and Logical Components of Zero Trust Architecture. Identify policy engine, administrator and enforcement point responsibilities.

assignment.title: An architecture decision with failure boundaries
instructions: Redesign the fictional notes service around resource-level identity checks, scoped workloads, protected secrets and segmented data access.
Draw policy decision/enforcement points and simulate their unavailability or stale policy using a decision table.
Compare two designs for usability, availability, privacy, cost and residual risk; no cloud deployment is needed.
acceptanceCriteria: Internal network placement grants no blanket authority.
The policy outage behavior is explicit and does not silently allow protected actions.
Trade-offs and an unaddressed residual risk are documented.

questions.prompt: Which statement best reflects zero-trust architecture principles?
choices: Evaluate scoped access rather than trusting network location alone
Require a VPN and trust every request after network entry
Repeat authentication but omit resource-level checks inside the network
questions.answer: Evaluate scoped access rather than trusting network location alone
questions.explanation: Zero trust is an architectural approach to decisions and enforcement, not a magic product or a promise of perfect security.

questions.prompt: Why consider policy-service availability in a security design?
questions.answer: If a dependency fails, systems must choose an explicit safe degraded mode; otherwise an outage can cause either uncontrolled access or unnecessary total failure.
questions.explanation: Security architecture includes fail-safe operation and availability, not only normal-case permission logic.

reviewPrompts: Where is policy decided, and where is that decision actually enforced?

lessons.title: Review architecture changes and evidence limitations
objectives: Update the threat model for new data, dependencies and actors.
Distinguish test evidence, design intent and unverified assumptions.

topics.title: Change impact
details: A new export, integration or service role can introduce a new boundary.
Supplier and privacy risks must be reviewed alongside application code.

topics.title: Assurance communication
details: Evidence has a date, scope, version and confidence.
A passing checklist does not prove the absence of unknown defects.
